newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Iscor slumps but analysts eye recovery.
newsitem.headline: Iscor slumps but analysts eye recovery.

text.p: Shares in South African iron and steel producer Iscor Ltd slumped on Wednesday, but analysts said they were already eyeing the recovery potential of the beleaguered stock.
The firm on Tuesday shocked the market by announcing a dismal set of first half results three weeks ahead of schedule. The figures came in lower than expected and triggered a huge sell-off.
Iscor shares quickly slumped to 325 cents, before edging up to stand at 339 cents by 1030 GMT, down nearly seven percent or 22 cents.
But analysts said the results -- showing a drop in pre-exceptional earnings per share to 6.5 cents from 17.6 cents -- represented the low point of the firm's economic cycle.
"A lot of people will now get out of the stock, but we are looking at the lowest earnings in this cycle. From here onwards earnings will grow," said one analyst who declined to be named.
Analysts said this gave the stock a great deal of recovery potential once the initial flurry of selling was over and the price consolidated at these low levels.
"The share price reaction is probably justified. But at this moment in time we should be looking through that," said SocGen Frankel Pollack analyst Troye Brady.
Analysts said the early announcement of the results had caught the market by surprise, but that such painful medicine was probably best taken sooner rather than later.
"From Iscor's point of view it was probably the best thing to do because there were all kinds of rumours floating around in the market," one analyst said.
The reasons for Iscor's poor performance stem from a difficult steel market both internationally and locally and a set of one-off problems specific to the firm.

The recommissioning of a blast furnace and continuous caster at its Vanderbijlpark Works and the commissioning of Pretoria Stainless Steel had hit the figures, but would not affect future financial results.
In the industry as a whole steel prices internationally have been bumping along the bottom of the cycle and in South Africa demand has also been hurt by the slowing down of the local economy.
But analysts said the outlook for the steel market was becoming brighter, with some predicting a recovery by 1998 or even sooner.

"We have seen de-stocking come to an end by the third quarter of last year both internationally and in South Africa. This will allow steel producers to start increasing their output levels and maybe their prices," Brady said.
The news from Iscor also hit Highveld Steel, which saw 50 cents shaved off its share price to stand at 19.25 rand. But analysts also saw Highveld as a recovery stock.
The firm has already issued a profit warning that likewise gave analysts a nasty shock and blamed a coming drop in profit on a mixture of tough market conditions and one-off circumstances.
Some analysts said the stock had more potential than Iscor due to its extensive vanadium operations. The outlook for vanadium, a metal used in many steel alloys, is bullish.
"We see Highveld in the same light. It could even be a little bit more of a recovery stock due to its vanadium operations," Brady said.
